d: The repetition of similar vowels in the stressed syllables of successive words
ety: From French assonance, from Latin assonāre; by surface analysis, a- + son- + -ance.
s: "You should try to speak without assonances" said Merlyn. "For instance, 'The beer is never clear round here, dear' is unfortunate, even as an assonance.'"

d: Medieval body armor that covers the chest and back
ety: First use appears c. 1464. From Middle English curasse, curesse, from Old French cuirace, spelling influenced by modern French cuirasse.
s: Lady Orkney's history, to whose house we are going, is a curious one. As Miss Elizabeth Villiers, by her charms she pierced the cuirass that enveloped the well-disciplined heart of William III.

d: A full supply
ety: From Middle English plenitude, that borrowed from Anglo-Norman plenitude, Middle French plenitude, and their source, Latin plēnitūdō.
s: Mankind's old greatness was created in scarcity. But what may we expect from plenitude?

d: A contradiction between two statements that seem equally reasonable
ety: Learned borrowing from Latin antinomia, from Ancient Greek ἀντινομία (antinomía), from ἀντι- (anti-, prefix meaning ‘against’) (ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₂ent- (“face; forehead; front”)) + νόμος (nómos, “custom, usage; law, ordinance”) + -ῐ́ᾱ (-ĭ́ā, suffix forming feminine abstract nouns), with νόμος (nómos) derived from νέμω (némō, “to deal out, dispense, distribute”) (from Proto-Indo
s: Of the work that has been done on the liar antinomy, possibly the most profound and certainly the most influential has been that of Tarski

d: Harmful to living things
ety: Adapted borrowing (1640s; 1582 as deletorious) of New Latin dēlētērius, dēlētōrius + -ous, from Ancient Greek δηλητήριος (dēlētḗrios, “noxious, deleterious”), from δηλητήρ (dēlētḗr, “a destroyer”), from δηλέομαι (dēléomai, “I hurt, damage, spoil, waste”). Not related to delete or deleble. Doublet of deletery.
s: Or might it suffice him, that every wholesome growth should be converted into something deleterious and malignant at his touch?

d: A basin for washing the hands (‘wash-hand basin’ is a British expression)
ety: From the Christian ritual, which was traditionally accompanied in Catholicism by a recitation of Psalm 25:6 (Psalm 26:6, in the Hebrew and in most modern translations) which in Latin begins with the word lavābō (“I will wash”). The sense of "room with a toilet" developed under the influence of lavatory and lav.
s: Mr. Pond fussed out and she heard the door of the little lavabo in the passage open with a loud creak.

d: Final honors degree examinations at Cambridge University
ety: Alteration of tripus, as though with a Greek ending. For the examination: the word is supposed to refer to the three-legged stool formerly used at the examinations for these honours, though some derive it from the three brackets formerly printed on the back of the paper. The etymon of tripus is the Ancient Greek τρίπους (trípous, “triple-footed”), (from τρι- (tri-, “three”) and πούς (poús, “foot”)
s: I'm seriously thinking of chucking my tripos and taking up the History Special.

d: A dagger with a slender blade
ety: From Middle English boydekin (“dagger”), apparently from *boyde, *boide (of unknown [Celtic?] origin) + -kin. Cognate with Scots botkin, boitkin, boikin (“bodkin”).
s: And can a man his own quietus make / with a bare bodkin? / With daggers, bodkins, bullets, man can make / a bruise or break of exit for his life; / but is that a quietus, O tell me, is it quietus?

d: The patterns of stress and intonation in a language
ety: From Middle French prosodie, from Latin prosōdia, from Ancient Greek προσῳδία (prosōidía, “song sung to music; pronunciation of syllable”), from πρός (prós, “to”) + ᾠδή (ōidḗ, “song”).
s: But the system of prosody in Samson plainly forbids extrametrical syllables in the midst of the line, and there is certainly no other example.

d: An infant’s repetition of sounds uttered by others
ety: From echo- + -lalia; echo- ultimately from Ancient Greek ἠχώ (ēkhṓ, “reflected sound, echo”), -lalia from λαλιά (laliá, “talk, chat”).
s: There was the boom of a bass drum, and the voice of the orchestra leader rang out suddenly above the echolalia of the garden.

d: A sophisticated person who has travelled in many countries
ety: Borrowed from French cosmopolite, from Latin cosmopolītēs, itself borrowed from Koine Greek κοσμοπολίτης (kosmopolítēs, “citizen of the world”), from Ancient Greek κόσμος (kósmos, “world”) + πολίτης (polítēs, “citizen”).
s: First drink a health, this solemn night, / A health to England, every guest: / That man’s the best cosmopolite / Who loves his native country best.

d: A windlass rotated in a horizontal plane around a vertical axis; used on ships for weighing anchor or raising heavy sails
ety: Borrowed into Middle English from either Old French cabestan, from Old Occitan cabestan, from cabestre (“pulley cord”) or from Spanish cabestran, both of which derive from Latin capistrum (“halter”), from capiō (“take hold of”).
s: We toiled over the capstan, and late in the afternoon slipped out of the harbour.

d: Something that bulges out or is protuberant or projects from its surroundings
ety: From Middle English, early 15th century, in sense “(action of) growing out (of something else)”. Borrowed from Latin excrescentia (“abnormal growths”), from excrescentem, from excrēscere, from ex- (“out”) (English ex-) + crēscere (“to grow”) (English crescent). Sense of “abnormal growth” from 1570s, from earlier excrescency (1540s in this sense).
s: Perhaps he meant that towns are after all excrescences, grey fluxions, where men, hurrying to find one another, have lost themselves.

d: A speech of violent denunciation
ety: From Latin philippicus, from Ancient Greek φιλιππικός (philippikós), from Φίλιππος (Phílippos, “lover of horses”), from φίλος (phílos, “loving”) + ἵππος (híppos, “horse”).
s: "Sir Robert Akhurst is a good man, a very good man, notwithstanding his philippic; but he is an old one, which makes all the difference."

d: Mix together different elements
ety: Attested since 1541: from Latin cōnflātus, past passive participle of cōnflō (“fuse, kindle, blow together”), see -ate (verb-forming suffix).
s: “Bacon was Lord Chancellor of England and the first European to experiment with gunpowder.” — “No, you are conflating Francis Bacon and Roger Bacon.”

d: A band of material around the waist that strengthens a skirt or trousers
ety: Learned borrowing from Latin cinctūra. Cognate with Spanish cintura (“waist”). Doublet of ceinture.
s: In one, dated eighteen years ago, he appeared, wearing only sandals and a cincture of vine leaves, between two classical garden statues.

d: Not fanciful or imaginative
ety: From Middle French prosaïque, from Medieval Latin prosaicus (“in prose”), from Latin prosa (“prose”), from prorsus (“straightforward, in prose”), from Old Latin provorsus (“straight ahead”), from pro- (“forward”) + vorsus (“turned”), from vertō (“to turn”), from Proto-Indo-European *wer- (“to turn, to bend”).
s: I was simply making the prosaic point that we are running late.

d: Having an agreeably pungent taste
ety: Borrowed from Middle French piquant (“pricking, stimulating, irritating”), present participle of piquer, possibly from Old French pikier (“to prick, sting, nettle”). Doublet of picong. Related to pike.
s: French charcuterie relies on cloves in the quatre épices, or four-spice powder, for seasoning fine sausages and piquant marinades.

d: A pert or flirtatious young girl
ety: Borrowed from French soubrette, from Occitan soubreta (“coy”) (feminine of soubret), from soubra (Provençal sobrar), from Latin superare (“be above”).
s: And then too it was exhilarating to see the baron come sailing in with a pair of soubrettes on his arm—each time a different pair.

d: A slight wind (usually refreshing)
ety: From Latin zephyrus (“west wind”), from Ancient Greek Ζέφυρος (Zéphuros). Doublet of zefir, zéphire, Zephyr, and Zephyrus. The confectionery sense is a semantic loan from Russian зефи́р (zefír).
s: The dusk of evening came on, soft in its solemnity, and unoppressive even in its gloom, under the sweet sky and unmolested zephyr, casting its pleasant shadows along the edges of the grove.

d: A display of bad temper
ety: Since 1833, from American English. Unknown origin, possibly a fanciful alteration of corruption, or maybe related to captious. Alternatively an arbitrary pseudo-Latinism coinage.
s: The joke was not that funny, but he went into conniptions laughing.

d: A woolen tunic worn by men and women in ancient Greece
ety: From Ancient Greek χιτών (khitṓn, “tunic”), from a Central Semitic *kittan, from the Akkadian 𒌆𒃰 (kitû, literally “flax, linen”), from Sumerian 𒄑𒃰 (kitû [GIŠ.GADA]).
s: She wears a diaphanous himation that covers her torso, over a floor-length chiton of heavier fabric.

d: Softly bright or radiant
ety: From Latin lambēns, present participle of lambō (“lick”).
s: We appreciated her lambent comments.

d: Unpleasantly and excessively suave or ingratiating in manner or speech
ety: Borrowed from French oléagineux, borrowed from Medieval Latin oleāginōsus (“oily”), from olea (“the olive tree or its fruit”).
s: The oleaginous salesman convinced me to buy a more expensive car.

d: Habitually speaking the truth
ety: From Latin vērāx (“truthful”) + -acious, from vērus (“true”).
s: Now there are two curious circumstances to be observed in this relation of my uncle's, who was, as I have said, a perfectly veracious man.

d: The straight line configuration of 3 celestial bodies (as the sun and earth and moon) in a gravitational system
ety: From Late Latin sȳzygia (“a conjunction”), from Ancient Greek συζυγία (suzugía, “a union, a yoke, a pair”). This word was recognized as English in 1847 (in its astronomical meaning).
s: The duration of an eclipse depends on the relative positions of the sun, moon, and earth in their syzygy.

d: Causing or able to cause nausea
ety: From Middle English noysom; equivalent to noy + -some (short for annoy, from an(n)oien, enoien from Anglo-Norman anuier, from Old French enuier (French ennuyer), from Late Latin inodiare, from in- (intensive prefix) + odium (“hate”)).
s: There is a distinct sense of freedom in the solitude of the night. The day's atmosphere is surcharged with noisome anxiety, the hours laden with impending terrors. But the night is soothing.

d: Extremely pleasing to the taste; sweet and fragrant
ety: Partly from ambrosia and partly from Latin ambrosius, + -al.
s: By your cheek of vermil hue, / By your lip’s ambrosial dew, / By your soft and languid eye, / By your swelling bosom’s sigh, / You taught me love.

d: Slang for a jail
ety: From informal spoken Spanish juzgao, variant of standard Spanish juzgado (“court, courthouse”). Alteration of pronunciation and spelling by law of Hobson-Jobson.
s: There's parts of Mexico they'd take you straight to the hoosegow for just whistlin that.

d: A railing at the side of a staircase or balcony to prevent people from falling
ety: Unadapted borrowing from French balustrade, from Italian balaustrata (“with balusters”), from balaustro (“baluster”), from balausta (“wild pomegranate flower”), via Latin balaustium, from Ancient Greek βαλαύστιον (balaústion), from Semitic, compare Classical Syriac ܒܠܳܨܳܐ (blāṣā, “pomegranate shoot”)). So named because of resemblance to the swelling form of the half-open pomegranate flower. Also s
s: The Jester sat down on one of the marble balustrades and regarded Alvin with a curious intentness.

d: An ornament (such as a knot of ribbon or a rosette) usually worn on the hat
ety: Partial calque of French cocarde.
s: The escort were two mounted patriots in red caps and tri-coloured cockades, armed with national muskets and sabres, who rode one on either side of him.

d: Especially fine or decorative clothing
ety: Aphetized from Middle English arayment, borrowed from Anglo-Norman arraiement and Old French areement, from areer (“to array”). See array.
s: We have entire schools dedicated to writing learned treatises on the beauty of the Emperor's raiment, and every major newspaper runs a section dedicated to imperial fashion...

d: Avoid and stay away from deliberately; stay clear of
ety: From Middle English eschewen, from Anglo-Norman eschiver, (third-person present eschiu), from Frankish *skiuhijan (“to dread, shun, avoid”); thus a doublet of skew. For the pronunciation with /ʃ/, compare the development of marshal from Middle English marschal (/marsˈt͡ʃaːl/) or Middle English myssheve, variant of myschef (“hardship”). Variants in /sk/ are either from unattested Middle English *es
s: What cannot be eschew'd must be embrac'd.

d: Loud confused noise from many sources
ety: Borrowed from French brouhaha, though its earlier origin is disputed. Possibly from Hebrew בָּרוּךְ הַבָּא (barúkh habá, “welcome”, literally “blessed is he who comes”).
s: It caused quite a brouhaha when the school suspended one of its top students for refusing to adhere to the dress code.

d: The necessary means (especially financial means)
ety: From where- + withal. Originally only an adverb, nominal use since ca. 1800.
s: I would like to help your project, but I do not have the wherewithal.

d: Someone shirking their duty by feigning illness or incapacity
ety: Inherited from Middle English sculkere; equivalent to skulk + -er. Compare Norwegian Nynorsk skulkar and Old Swedish skulkare.
s: Afterwards he was again taken by Ethiopian Skulkers, and carry’d away into the Maritime Parts of Ethiopia.

d: A thin plain-weave cotton or linen fabric; used for shirts or dresses
ety: From French batiste, a form of Baptiste, of disputed origin (“according to Littré and Scheler from the alleged original maker, Baptiste of Cambray; according to others, from its use in wiping the heads of children after baptism” – OED).
s: He had started to stroke her, shivering, staring ahead, following with a blind man's hand the dip of her spine through the batiste.

d: A deceptive maneuver (especially to avoid capture)
ety: From Middle French artifice, from Latin artificium.
s: The notion that consequence can be as easily managed as PR is the ultimate artifice and the ultimate delusion.

d: An important person in India
ety: Borrowed from Urdu سردار, Hindi सरदार (sardār), from Persian سردار (sardâr). Doublet of serdar and Sardar.
s: Sir Reginald, as Sirdar of the Egyptian Army, had been put in command of the British military side of the Arab adventure in place of Sir Henry McMahon

d: Too obvious to be doubted
ety: Either from French indubitable or Latin indubitābilis. By surface analysis, in- + dubitable.
s: The indubitable effect of the potion convinced many nonbelievers.
